about.title: Chula Vista Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Chula Vista is home to more than 265,000 people, and most of them spend part of every day on property someone else controls: shopping centers along Broadway and Main Street, apartment complexes off Olympic Parkway, storefronts and offices near 4th Avenue. When a property owner lets a hazard sit, the person who gets hurt is rarely the one at fault. Still, California law puts a specific burden on the injured person. You generally have to show the owner knew about the hazard, or reasonably should have known, and did not fix it or warn about it. That is why what you do in the first days matters so much. Photos of the spill, the loose tile, or the unlit stairwell, taken before anything is cleaned up, carry real weight. So does surveillance footage, which many San Diego County businesses overwrite within days or weeks. LawProactive is not a law firm. We simply connect you, free of charge, with an independent Chula Vista-area attorney who can send a preservation request and start building the record before it disappears.

whyChoose.title: Why Chula Vista Residents Use LawProactive for Fall Claims

items.title: Notice is the whole case, and it needs early work
items.desc: Premises claims in California turn on proving the owner knew or should have known about the hazard. An attorney can request maintenance logs, incident reports, and prior complaints while those records still exist.

items.title: Video disappears fast
items.desc: Stores, gyms, and apartment buildings routinely overwrite security footage on a short cycle. The attorney you are connected with can send a written preservation demand right away so the footage of your fall is not lost.

items.title: Deadlines vary, and the public-entity one is short
items.desc: Most premises claims carry a two-year filing deadline in California, but a fall on city, school, or county property triggers a much shorter government claim window. Getting connected early keeps every option open.

items.question: I fell at a Chula Vista shopping center but wasn't sure how badly I was hurt. Did I wait too long?
items.answer: Probably not. California generally allows two years from the date of a fall to file a premises liability lawsuit against a private owner. That said, evidence such as surveillance video and cleaning logs can vanish long before the legal deadline, so reaching out sooner gives an attorney a better chance of preserving it. If the fall happened on public property, a government claim may need to be filed within months, so check quickly.

items.question: The store says I should have watched where I was going. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: No. California follows pure comparative fault, which means a claim can still go forward even if you are found partly responsible. Your recovery would be reduced by your share of fault rather than eliminated. An attorney can push back on blame-shifting by showing the hazard was one the owner should have addressed.

items.question: What should I do right after a fall on someone else's property?
items.answer: Get medical care first, then document everything you can: photos of the hazard, the lighting, your footwear, and any visible injuries. Ask that an incident report be written and request a copy. Note the names of any witnesses or employees, and avoid giving a recorded statement to an insurer until you have spoken with an attorney. LawProactive can connect you with one free of charge.
